questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: The mass spectrum of an element contains singly charged isotope-ion peaks at m/z 63 and 65. Their relative abundances are respectively 69.0% and 31.0%. (a) Explain the meaning of m/z. (b) Calculate the relative atomic mass using the abundances. (c) Which ion reaches the TOF detector first when both ions have the same kinetic energy and charge? Explain why.
markPoints: m/z means mass divided by charge number; for singly charged isotope ions it is their relative ion mass.
Use the weighted mean: Ar=[63(69.0)+65(31.0)]/100.
The relative atomic mass is Ar=63.62 (approximately 63.6).
The m/z 63 ion arrives first because it has smaller mass; at equal kinetic energy it travels faster, so t=L/v is shorter.
questions.modelAnswer: m/z means mass divided by charge number; for singly charged isotope ions it is their relative ion mass. Use the weighted mean: Ar=[63(69.0)+65(31.0)]/100. The relative atomic mass is Ar=63.62 (approximately 63.6). The m/z 63 ion arrives first because it has smaller mass; at equal kinetic energy it travels faster, so t=L/v is shorter.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: A student uses a simple time-of-flight mass spectrometer to analyse the isotopes of a metal. Describe the four main stages from ionisation to mass-spectrum output. Explain why vacuum is important and why ions of lower mass and the same charge arrive first when ions receive the same kinetic energy. Your answer must distinguish the horizontal and vertical axes of the resulting spectrum.
markPoints: Ionisation converts sample particles to positive ions.
Electron-impact ionisation can remove an electron from gaseous particles; ions can also be formed by electrospray.
An electric field accelerates positive ions and, in the simple equal-charge model, gives them equal kinetic energies.
Ions travel through a field-free drift region of fixed length.
A vacuum reduces collisions that would change ion paths or energy.
At equal KE=½mv² a lighter ion has a greater speed, so it reaches the detector sooner.
Ion arrival generates a signal at the detector; signal intensity is related to ion abundance.
The spectrum plots m/z on the horizontal axis and relative abundance/intensity on the vertical axis.

An electric field accelerates positive ions and, in the simple equal-charge model, gives them equal kinetic energies. Ions travel through a field-free drift region of fixed length. A vacuum reduces collisions that would change ion paths or energy. At equal KE=½mv² a lighter ion has a greater speed, so it reaches the detector sooner. Ion arrival generates a signal at the detector; signal intensity is related to ion abundance. The spectrum plots m/z on the horizontal axis and relative abundance/intensity on the vertical axis.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: A singly charged positive ion of mass 3.98×10⁻²⁶ kg receives a kinetic energy of 1.99×10⁻¹⁶ J before entering a 1.20 m field-free flight tube. (a) Calculate the speed of the ion. (b) Calculate its flight time. (c) A second singly charged isotope ion has mass 4.31×10⁻²⁶ kg and the same kinetic energy. Determine its flight time and explain the result. Give appropriate units.
markPoints: Use kinetic energy E=½mv² and rearrange to v=√(2E/m).
Flight time of the first ion is t=1.20/(1.00×10⁵)=1.20×10⁻⁵ s.
For the second ion speed v₂=√(2×1.99×10⁻¹⁶/(4.31×10⁻²⁶))≈9.61×10⁴ m s⁻¹.
Second flight time =1.20/(9.61×10⁴)≈1.25×10⁻⁵ s.
The second ion is heavier and thus slower at equal kinetic energy; it has a longer flight time.
questions.modelAnswer: Use kinetic energy E=½mv² and rearrange to v=√(2E/m). For the first ion v=√(2×1.99×10⁻¹⁶/(3.98×10⁻²⁶))=1.00×10⁵ m s⁻¹. Flight time of the first ion is t=1.20/(1.00×10⁵)=1.20×10⁻⁵ s. For the second ion speed v₂=√(2×1.99×10⁻¹⁶/(4.31×10⁻²⁶))≈9.61×10⁴ m s⁻¹. Second flight time =1.20/(9.61×10⁴)≈1.25×10⁻⁵ s. The second ion is heavier and thus slower at equal kinetic energy; it has a longer flight time.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: An element has three singly charged isotopes: mass 54 with 5.8% abundance, mass 56 with 91.7% abundance, and mass 57 with 2.5% abundance. (a) Calculate the element's relative atomic mass. (b) Explain why the relative atomic mass is not a whole number. (c) Predict which ion arrives last in a simple TOF instrument with equal KE.
markPoints: Contributions are 313.2, 5135.2 and 142.5 respectively.
The result Ar=55.909, or about 55.9.
The value is non-integer because it is an abundance-weighted mean of different isotopes.
The mass-57 ion arrives last because it is the heaviest singly charged ion and therefore slowest at equal KE.
questions.modelAnswer: Weighted mean = (54×5.8 + 56×91.7 + 57×2.5)/100. Contributions are 313.2, 5135.2 and 142.5 respectively. The result Ar=55.909, or about 55.9. The value is non-integer because it is an abundance-weighted mean of different isotopes. The mass-57 ion arrives last because it is the heaviest singly charged ion and therefore slowest at equal KE.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: An organic compound of relative molecular mass 72 is examined by both electron-impact ionisation and electrospray. In the electron-impact spectrum a peak is present at m/z 72 and an intense peak at m/z 43. In an electrospray spectrum, a singly charged [M+H]⁺ peak is present. (a) Explain the two methods of ion formation. (b) Predict the electrospray m/z. (c) Explain why m/z 43 could be the base peak rather than the molecular ion.
markPoints: Electron impact removes an electron, forming a positive molecular ion M⁺• (with fragmentation possible).
The intact singly charged EI molecular ion is at m/z 72.
Electrospray often protonates the molecule, forming [M+H]⁺.
Electrospray protonated molecular ion is at m/z approximately 73.
The m/z 43 ion can be a charged fragment of the molecule.
The base peak is the most intense signal, not necessarily the intact molecular ion.
questions.modelAnswer: Electron impact removes an electron, forming a positive molecular ion M⁺• (with fragmentation possible). The intact singly charged EI molecular ion is at m/z 72. Electrospray often protonates the molecule, forming [M+H]⁺. Electrospray protonated molecular ion is at m/z approximately 73. The m/z 43 ion can be a charged fragment of the molecule. The base peak is the most intense signal, not necessarily the intact molecular ion.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: A metal ion of relative mass 48 carries a 2+ charge. Another metal ion of relative mass 24 carries a 1+ charge. (a) Calculate the m/z for both ions. (b) Explain whether the two ions have distinguishable m/z values. (c) If accelerated through the same potential difference, explain how their gained kinetic energies differ, using the charge–voltage relationship.
markPoints: For the 48-mass 2+ ion, m/z=48/2=24.
For the 24-mass 1+ ion, m/z=24/1=24.
Both have the same m/z value, so they are not resolved by their m/z alone.
Energy gained on acceleration is E=qV.
The 2+ ion gains twice as much kinetic energy as the 1+ ion at the same accelerating voltage.
Even though their energies differ, ideal TOF time depends on m/z for ions through the same voltage.
questions.modelAnswer: For the 48-mass 2+ ion, m/z=48/2=24. For the 24-mass 1+ ion, m/z=24/1=24. Both have the same m/z value, so they are not resolved by their m/z alone. Energy gained on acceleration is E=qV. The 2+ ion gains twice as much kinetic energy as the 1+ ion at the same accelerating voltage. Even though their energies differ, ideal TOF time depends on m/z for ions through the same voltage.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: An ion is represented as ⁵⁶₂₆Fe³⁺. A second atom is ⁵⁷₂₆Fe and a third is ⁵⁶₂₇Co. (a) Determine protons, neutrons and electrons in the iron ion. (b) Explain which two species are isotopes. (c) Explain why the cobalt species is not an isotope of iron. (d) Define isotope.
markPoints: Iron has 26 protons because Z=26.
Number of neutrons in ⁵⁶Fe³⁺ is A−Z=56−26=30.
Number of electrons in Fe³⁺ is 26−3=23.
⁵⁶Fe and ⁵⁷Fe are isotopes; they share Z=26 but differ in neutron numbers.
⁵⁶Co has Z=27, so it is a different element, not an iron isotope.
Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same protons but different neutrons.
questions.modelAnswer: Iron has 26 protons because Z=26. Number of neutrons in ⁵⁶Fe³⁺ is A−Z=56−26=30. Number of electrons in Fe³⁺ is 26−3=23. ⁵⁶Fe and ⁵⁷Fe are isotopes; they share Z=26 but differ in neutron numbers. ⁵⁶Co has Z=27, so it is a different element, not an iron isotope. Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same protons but different neutrons.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: An isotope of an element has 17 protons and 20 neutrons. It forms a 1− ion. (a) Write the nuclear symbol (including A and Z). (b) Determine the number of electrons in its 1− ion. (c) Explain why isotopes of this element react chemically in almost the same way. (d) State the definition of relative atomic mass, Ar.
markPoints: Element with Z=17 is chlorine, Cl.
Mass number A=17+20=37, giving ³⁷₁₇Cl.
A chloride ion Cl− has gained one electron and contains 18 electrons.
Isotopes of the same element have the same electronic configuration, so their chemical properties are very similar.
Ar is the weighted mean mass of an atom of the element relative to 1/12 of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.
questions.modelAnswer: Element with Z=17 is chlorine, Cl. Mass number A=17+20=37, giving ³⁷₁₇Cl. A chloride ion Cl− has gained one electron and contains 18 electrons. Isotopes of the same element have the same electronic configuration, so their chemical properties are very similar. Ar is the weighted mean mass of an atom of the element relative to 1/12 of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: Explain how experimental evidence changed the model of the atom from the plum-pudding model to a nuclear atom. A beam of positively charged alpha particles is directed at a very thin sheet of metal foil; most pass through, a few scatter at large angles, and a very small number are scattered backwards. Account for all three observations.
markPoints: The earlier plum-pudding model had electrons embedded in a diffuse positive charge.
Most alpha particles pass through because atoms are mostly empty space.
A small proportion undergo large-angle scattering when they approach concentrated positive nuclear charge.
A very small number scatter backwards following close approaches to a tiny dense positive nucleus.
This evidence supports a small, dense, positively charged nucleus instead of diffuse positive charge.
questions.modelAnswer: The earlier plum-pudding model had electrons embedded in a diffuse positive charge. Most alpha particles pass through because atoms are mostly empty space. A small proportion undergo large-angle scattering when they approach concentrated positive nuclear charge. A very small number scatter backwards following close approaches to a tiny dense positive nucleus. This evidence supports a small, dense, positively charged nucleus instead of diffuse positive charge.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: Write the full electron configurations of Fe, Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺ using a noble-gas core where appropriate. Explain why 4s electrons are removed before 3d electrons on ionisation, despite the 4s subshell normally filling before 3d.
markPoints: Neutral iron has configuration [Ar]3d⁶4s².
Fe²⁺ has [Ar]3d⁶, losing two 4s electrons.
Fe³⁺ has [Ar]3d⁵ after a further electron is lost from 3d.
Neutral iron fills 4s before 3d.
Once 3d is occupied, 4s is higher in energy for forming these ions, so 4s electrons are removed first.
All configurations have correct total electrons for the stated charge.
questions.modelAnswer: Neutral iron has configuration [Ar]3d⁶4s². Fe²⁺ has [Ar]3d⁶, losing two 4s electrons. Fe³⁺ has [Ar]3d⁵ after a further electron is lost from 3d. Neutral iron fills 4s before 3d. Once 3d is occupied, 4s is higher in energy for forming these ions, so 4s electrons are removed first. All configurations have correct total electrons for the stated charge.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: Explain why first ionisation energy generally increases across Period 3 (Na to Ar), and explain specifically why the first ionisation energy decreases from Mg to Al and from P to S. Reference subshells, shielding, attraction and electron repulsion in your answer.
markPoints: Across Period 3 the number of protons (nuclear charge) increases.
Electrons added across the period occupy the same principal shell, so shielding changes comparatively little.
Stronger effective nuclear attraction generally increases first ionisation energy.
Al loses a higher-energy 3p electron whereas Mg loses a lower-energy 3s electron.
The 3p electron in Al is easier to remove, so Al's first IE is lower than Mg's.
P has three singly occupied 3p orbitals, whereas S has a pair of electrons in one 3p orbital.
Paired-electron repulsion in the S 3p orbital makes removal of one electron easier, so S has lower first IE than P.
questions.modelAnswer: Across Period 3 the number of protons (nuclear charge) increases. Electrons added across the period occupy the same principal shell, so shielding changes comparatively little. Stronger effective nuclear attraction generally increases first ionisation energy. Al loses a higher-energy 3p electron whereas Mg loses a lower-energy 3s electron. The 3p electron in Al is easier to remove, so Al's first IE is lower than Mg's. P has three singly occupied 3p orbitals, whereas S has a pair of electrons in one 3p orbital. Paired-electron repulsion in the S 3p orbital makes removal of one electron easier, so S has lower first IE than P.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: The first four ionisation energies of an element (in kJ mol⁻¹) are 738, 1451, 7733 and 10543. (a) Explain what is meant by first and second ionisation energy. (b) Write correct general equations for both. (c) Deduce the number of outer-shell electrons and likely periodic-table group. (d) Explain the large jump.
markPoints: First ionisation removes one electron from each atom in one mole of gaseous atoms to form 1+ gaseous ions.
Second ionisation removes one electron from each ion in one mole of gaseous 1+ ions to form 2+ gaseous ions.
First ionisation equation: X(g) → X⁺(g) + e⁻.
Second ionisation equation: X⁺(g) → X²⁺(g) + e⁻.
Large jump is after the second electron is removed, showing two outer-shell electrons.
Element is in Group 2 (data consistent with magnesium).
The third electron would be removed from an inner shell closer to the nucleus and less shielded.
Successive ionisation energies increase due to greater positive charge on the remaining ion.
questions.modelAnswer: First ionisation removes one electron from each atom in one mole of gaseous atoms to form 1+ gaseous ions. Second ionisation removes one electron from each ion in one mole of gaseous 1+ ions to form 2+ gaseous ions. First ionisation equation: X(g) → X⁺(g) + e⁻. Second ionisation equation: X⁺(g) → X²⁺(g) + e⁻. Large jump is after the second electron is removed, showing two outer-shell electrons. Element is in Group 2 (data consistent with magnesium). The third electron would be removed from an inner shell closer to the nucleus and less shielded. Successive ionisation energies increase due to greater positive charge on the remaining ion.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: Explain the trend in first ionisation energy down Group 2 from Be to Ba. In your answer, explain the roles of nuclear charge, atomic radius, shielding and the distance of the electron removed. State whether the trend is an overall increase or decrease.
markPoints: First ionisation energy generally decreases down Group 2.
Additional occupied electron shells increase atomic radius and outer-electron distance from the nucleus.
Inner electron shells provide increased shielding.
Nuclear charge also increases down the group, but shielding and distance dominate.
The attractive force experienced by the outer electron is reduced, so less energy is needed to remove it.
questions.modelAnswer: First ionisation energy generally decreases down Group 2. Additional occupied electron shells increase atomic radius and outer-electron distance from the nucleus. Inner electron shells provide increased shielding. Nuclear charge also increases down the group, but shielding and distance dominate. The attractive force experienced by the outer electron is reduced, so less energy is needed to remove it.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: Write the ground-state electron configurations of chromium, copper and the chloride ion using [Ar] where possible. Explain the exception to the simple 4s²3dⁿ filling pattern in chromium and copper. State the capacity of an s, p and d subshell.
markPoints: Chromium is [Ar]3d⁵4s¹.
Copper is [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹.
Chloride ion Cl− contains 18 electrons and is [Ar].
Cr adopts the energetically favourable half-filled d⁵ configuration.
Cu adopts the energetically favourable completely filled d¹⁰ configuration.
Maximum occupancies are s=2, p=6 and d=10 electrons.
questions.modelAnswer: Chromium is [Ar]3d⁵4s¹. Copper is [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹. Chloride ion Cl− contains 18 electrons and is [Ar]. Cr adopts the energetically favourable half-filled d⁵ configuration. Cu adopts the energetically favourable completely filled d¹⁰ configuration. Maximum occupancies are s=2, p=6 and d=10 electrons.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.series: Original AQA-style Period 3 ionisation energy question
questions.prompt: The first ionisation energies of four Period 3 elements are: Mg 738 kJ mol⁻¹, Al 578 kJ mol⁻¹, P 1012 kJ mol⁻¹ and S 1000 kJ mol⁻¹. The general trend across Period 3 is an increase in first ionisation energy. Explain the general trend and account for both decreases from Mg to Al and P to S. Refer to electron subshells and electron pairing in your explanation. [5 marks]
markPoints: Nuclear charge increases across Period 3 because proton number rises.
Outer electrons are added to the same principal shell, so shielding stays approximately constant and the stronger nuclear attraction usually raises the first ionisation energy.
Aluminium loses a higher-energy 3p electron, whereas magnesium loses a lower-energy 3s electron, making aluminium's first ionisation energy lower.
Phosphorus has three singly occupied 3p orbitals, whereas sulfur has two electrons paired in one 3p orbital.
Repulsion between the paired 3p electrons in sulfur makes one electron easier to remove, so the first ionisation energy of S is below P.
questions.modelAnswer: Nuclear charge increases across Period 3 because proton number rises. Outer electrons are added to the same principal shell, so shielding stays approximately constant and the stronger nuclear attraction usually raises the first ionisation energy. Aluminium loses a higher-energy 3p electron, whereas magnesium loses a lower-energy 3s electron, making aluminium's first ionisation energy lower. Phosphorus has three singly occupied 3p orbitals, whereas sulfur has two electrons paired in one 3p orbital. Repulsion between the paired 3p electrons in sulfur makes one electron easier to remove, so the first ionisation energy of S is below P.
